name: Liam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run the front office at Eastgate Community Health Centre, a clinic just off Station Road with six doctors and four nurses. I'm in by eight, clear the overnight voicemails, rebook the people who can't make it, and sort the referral letters into the right trays. I still keep a paper diary next to the booking system, because the system has crashed twice this year and the diary saved us both times.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every regular by name, like Mr Okafor who comes in every Tuesday for his bloods and always brings the receptionists biscuits. What wears me out is the software updates, honestly. Every few months the screens move around and I lose a week getting my speed back. I've never touched the AI chat things, and I'm not planning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Half my union branch has been warning that the AI talk was mostly sales pitch. I'd post something like that in the branch group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not completely. The clinic already trialled a booking bot last spring and it sent three diabetic patients to the wrong day. Even a small bit of automation lands right on my desk, because my whole day is booking, filing and letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep the paper diary going. I'd still go to the union meetings on the first Thursday of the month, because the managers would push whatever bits of software they'd paid for anyway. And I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small itch. A clinic that runs on a paper diary when the computer crashes doesn't need a robot. The clinic needs someone who answers the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the booking bot trial. What happened with that, and who decided it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice manager, Gail, signed it off after a sales visit. It lasted four months and they quietly switched it off after the complaints. Nobody asked the front desk before it went in, which is the bit that still annoys me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With your savings and plenty of similar jobs nearby, is anything about this picture on your mind at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. Dev, my partner, is a nurse at the hospital, so between us we're steady and we've got about nine months of pay put by. The only thing is that managers like Gail will keep buying gadgets, even if they're useless, and I'm the one who has to clean up after them.

say: I'd tell my **union branch** the AI talk was mostly a sales pitch all along.
I'd say the clinic still runs on **people answering phones**, not software.
think: Even small **booking automation** lands on my desk, because my whole day is booking and filing.
The failed **booking bot trial** shows managers will still buy tools without asking the front desk.
do: Keep running the **paper diary** alongside the booking system as a backup.
Attend the **monthly union meeting** to watch what software management buys next.
Keep the usual **monthly saving** going with no changes.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small itch about managers buying more gadgets.
S0.quote: A clinic that runs on a paper diary when the computer crashes doesn't need a robot. The clinic needs someone who answers the phone.
fieldNote: Liam's **resistance** to new tech is practical, rooted in two system crashes the paper diary covered.
The real irritation is about **not being consulted**, more than about AI itself.
Strong savings and a **nurse partner** make him feel secure in this picture.

steps.text: Keep the paper diary going beside the clinic booking system
Raise the booking bot complaints at the monthly union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement before any of this goes in, written down, with the union at the table. Online I'd probably share the union's statement rather than write my own. I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one that sounds real. Booking, letters, answering patients, chasing referrals, that's the list on the card and it's basically my job description. I think the clinic would keep one person at the desk instead of three, and I'm not sure it'd be me, because I'm the one who won't touch the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Gail early and ask what the plan is for the front office, and I'd get the union rep in on that meeting. I'd stop the extra spending I'd planned, like the new bike, and put that into savings. If the clinic started cutting, I'd look at the hospital's medical records department, because records still need someone handling the actual paper files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I keep thinking about the morning the booking bot went wrong and patients were standing at the counter angry, and picturing that as the normal day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the new tools. Would that change if your job depended on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if they trained us properly in work hours. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it. I've watched software tell a diabetic patient to come on the wrong day, so I'm not going to trust software with someone's insulin review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the clinic would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious, who does the evening shift on reception. She's 58 and she's never going to retrain into something else. I'd want the union pushing for her first, honestly, before me.

say: I'd demand a **written agreement** with the union before any new software goes into the clinic.
Online I'd share the **union statement** rather than writing my own posts.
think: The card's list of tasks is basically my **job description**, line for line.
The clinic might keep **one person** at the desk, and refusing the tools could make me the one cut.
do: Ask the practice manager for the **front office plan**, with the union rep in the room.
Shift the planned **bike money** into savings instead.
Look at **medical records** jobs at the hospital if cuts start.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into real worry about patients and his own desk.
Protective of an **older colleague** who couldn't retrain.
S1.quote: I've watched software tell a diabetic patient to come on the wrong day, so I'm not going to trust software with someone's insulin review.
fieldNote: Liam sees his whole **daily task list** on the Steady Disruption card and says so directly.
He knows his **refusal to use AI** could single him out, yet still won't commit to learning it.
His concern for **patient safety** is his main argument, more than his own job.

steps.text: Ask the practice manager for the front office plan with the union rep
Put the new bike money into the savings account instead
Check vacancies in the hospital's medical records department

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that governments let tech companies do this to everyone without asking. I'd be at whatever protest the unions organised in town. I'd post that one, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone within a year of that. If the AI can do any thinking work as well as a person, then booking and filing is the first thing out the door. The only bit left would be standing at the counter, and that's not a full-time wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for hands-on work right away, because robots come three years later and that's three years of pay. The hospital porters and the stores department move actual things around, so I'd apply there. I'd also stop all spending except bills and food, and Dev and I would hold off on buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I feel like I'd be running out of the building just as the robots are coming in the back door, three years behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings. How long would they carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months of my pay, maybe a year if we're careful. With Dev still working we'd be fine for a while. Nine months of savings sounds like a lot until you realise every office job in town disappears the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years until robots can do hands-on work. What does that gap mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means portering is a stopgap, not a career. I'd take it and hope the unions get some kind of public support scheme sorted in those three years. Somebody has to pay people when there's no work, and it should be the companies making the money.

say: I'd blame **governments and tech firms** for letting this happen without asking anyone.
I'd join any **union protest** in town and post about that one.
think: Booking and filing would be the **first work gone**, probably within a year.
Only the **counter work** would be left, and that's not a full-time wage.
do: Apply for **porter or stores** jobs at the hospital straight away.
Cut all spending except **bills and food**.
Put the **flat purchase** with his partner on hold.
feel: **Scared**, like running out the front as robots come in the back three years later.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings sounds like a lot until you realise every office job in town disappears the same week.
fieldNote: Liam expects to **lose his job** within a year and is already planning his exit.
He treats hands-on hospital work as a **three-year stopgap**, not an answer.
His answer to the gap is **public support** paid for by companies, true to his politics.

steps.text: Apply for porter or stores jobs at the hospital
Cut spending to bills and food only
Put the flat purchase with Dev on hold
Join the union protest against unchecked AI rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly the time for unions to get organised, while there's still a few years. I'd push our branch to put this on every agenda. I might even stand for branch rep, which I've always ducked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds better than two but it's the same ending for me. My job's pure desk work, so I don't get the extra three years that hands-on people get. I'd have maybe four good years at the clinic before it starts to empty out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the union's health and safety rep course, because that gives me some protection and a skill. I'd keep saving hard, maybe a quarter of my pay instead of a tenth. And I'd look properly at training as a healthcare assistant, which is hands-on and close to what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but not frozen. Five years gives me time to train for something with my hands, which I never thought I'd say as an office person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Healthcare assistant is a big switch. What would Dev say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would laugh first, because I go pale at blood tests. Then Dev would say do it, because the nurses always need hands. Dev's been telling me for years I'm wasted behind a counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you dislike new tools. Would you learn the AI systems in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. But if the AI does the whole thinking job by 2031, learning to use it for three years doesn't save me. I'd rather put the time into the thing it can't do yet.

say: I'd push my union branch to **get organised** while there are still a few years.
I might finally stand for **branch rep**, which I've always avoided.
think: Pure desk work means I don't get the **extra three years** hands-on people get.
Five years still ends with the clinic office **emptying out** around 2031.
do: Take the union's **health and safety rep** course in the first year.
Raise saving from about a tenth to a **quarter of pay**.
Look into training as a **healthcare assistant**.
feel: **Tense** but able to act, surprised to be planning hands-on work.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to train for something with my hands, which I never thought I'd say as an office person.
fieldNote: Liam reasons clearly that his **desk-only job** gets no robot delay.
He refuses to **learn AI tools** because he thinks they won't save him, not out of fear alone.
Moving to **healthcare assistant** work is a bold step for someone who avoids change.

steps.text: Take the union's health and safety rep course
Save a quarter of each pay packet instead of a tenth
Apply for healthcare assistant training at the hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do it properly, with retraining paid for and a proper safety net. I'd say that at work and I'd write to our local representative. That's a fair ask with a decade to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough for me to actually change track without panicking. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives and 40 when the robots do. That's still young enough to have built something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the clinic for now, because it's a good job and I like it. In year one I'd start part-time evening classes towards a healthcare assistant certificate, and carry on saving the usual amount. I'd keep going to the union and push for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but it's still there in the back of my head. Ten years means I can learn a hands-on trade slowly, instead of jumping into one scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the usual savings. Why not more, like in the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I want a normal life too. Dev and I want the flat. I'd rather buy the flat now and have it paid down a bit by the time it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Precious, your colleague, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she'll probably reach retirement before the desk disappears, which is true at 58. I'd still make sure the union looks after the people in the middle, the ones in their forties. They're the ones who'd get squeezed.

say: I'd ask for **paid retraining** and a proper safety net, since there's a decade to plan.
I'd write to our **local representative** about it.
think: Ten years means I'd be **37 and 40** when AI and robots land, still young enough.
There's time to **change track** without panicking.
do: Stay at the **clinic job** for now, since it's good work.
Start **evening classes** towards a healthcare assistant certificate in year one.
Push the union for a **retraining fund**.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, though the worry stays at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can learn a hands-on trade slowly, instead of jumping into one scared.
fieldNote: With a decade, Liam balances **normal life plans** like the flat against preparing.
He still sees his **desk job ending**, so the worry doesn't go away.
His politics show in a steady push for a **retraining fund**.

steps.text: Enrol in evening classes for a healthcare assistant certificate
Write to the local representative about a public retraining fund
Keep working the clinic front desk as normal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. There's no time to train for anything, and my whole job is the stuff it does first. What would help is the hospital and the unions setting up paid retraining into care work, so people like me could switch without losing a year's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets asked. Nobody asked the front desk about the booking bot. Nobody asks the receptionist before buying the software, and the receptionist is the one who fixes the mess afterwards.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the receptionist before buying the software, and the receptionist is the one who fixes the mess afterwards.
portrait: Liam is a 27-year-old **clinic receptionist** who keeps a paper diary because the system has crashed twice.
He's a committed **union member** who never uses AI tools and dislikes software changes.
He feels secure in AI Plateau but sees his **job description** in Steady Disruption.
In the AGI pictures he plans a move into **hands-on hospital work**, faster the less time there is.
He blames **tech firms and governments** and wants paid retraining and a safety net.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain and his work goes first.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** into care work, set up by the hospital and unions, without losing a year's pay.
